title: Space Stations Before the ISS
summary: Before the International Space Station, the Soviet Union and the United States built and tested earlier space stations, including Salyut, Skylab, and Mir, learning hard lessons along the way.
poll: Building the very first space station was harder than building the ISS.

versions.title: Space Stations Before the ISS
versions.text:
Space stations are homes in space. Three of them came before the ISS.

Long ago, no one lived in space. Then people had a new idea. They could build a home. It could fly around Earth.

The first space station was Salyut 1. It went up in 1971. A crew moved inside it.

Next came Skylab. The United States built it. It launched in 1973. Part of it broke. The crew had to repair it. Three crews lived there and did tests.

Then came Mir. It was much bigger. It launched in 1986. New parts were added for years. One crew member stayed in orbit for over a year.

These stations taught us a lot. Crews learned to live, work, and repair things in space.

Later, people built a new station. It is called the ISS. It uses ideas from Salyut, Skylab, and Mir. It still flies today.

versions.title: Space Stations Before the ISS
versions.text:
Space stations are homes that fly in space. Three of them came before the ISS.

Long ago, no one lived in space. Then people had a big idea. They could build a home. It could fly around Earth again and again. We call this a space station.

The first one was named Salyut 1. It was sent up in 1971. A crew flew up and moved inside. It was the first home in orbit.

Next, a new station went up. It was called Skylab. It launched in 1973. Part of it broke. The crew had to repair it. Three crews lived there. They studied the Sun. They tested how space changes the body.

Then came an even bigger station. It was called Mir. It launched in 1986. New parts were added for years. One crew member stayed in orbit for over a year! Visitors came from far away too.

These early stations taught us a lot. Crews learned how to live, work, and fix things far from home.

Years later, people built a new station. They used ideas from the three early ones. It is called the ISS. It still flies today.

versions.title: Space Stations Before the ISS
versions.text:
Space stations are homes that fly around Earth. Three of them came long before the ISS.

Long ago, no people lived in space at all. Then scientists had a bold idea. They could build a home that flies around Earth again and again. We call this kind of home a space station.

The first space station was Salyut 1. It was launched in 1971 by the Soviets. A crew flew up in a small ship and moved inside. It was the first home for people in orbit. Sadly, the crew died on the trip home.

Next came a station called Skylab. It launched in 1973. During launch, part of its shield broke off. The inside grew dangerously hot. The first crew had to repair the damage fast. After the fix, three crews lived on Skylab. They studied the Sun and tested how space changes the body.

After that came a much bigger station called Mir. It launched in 1986. Workers kept adding new parts for many years. One crew member stayed in orbit for over a year! Later, visitors came from far away too.

These early stations taught people many lessons about living, working, and making repairs far from home.

Years later, engineers built a new station. They used ideas from Salyut, Skylab, and Mir. It is called the ISS. It still flies today.

versions.title: Space Stations Before the ISS
versions.text:
Space stations are homes that fly around Earth. Several of them came long before the ISS existed.

Long before anyone lived in space, scientists had a bold idea. They could build a home that flies around Earth again and again. We call this kind of home a space station.

The first space station was Salyut 1. The Soviets sent it into orbit in 1971. A crew flew up in a small ship and moved inside. It was humanity's first home in orbit. Sadly, its crew died on the trip back to Earth. More Salyut stations followed. Later ones stayed in orbit for years.

Next came a station called Skylab, launched in 1973. During launch, part of its sunshield tore away. The inside grew dangerously hot. The first crew had to repair the damage fast. Three crews lived on Skylab. They studied the Sun and tested how space changes the body. In 1979, Skylab ran out of fuel. It fell back through the sky and broke apart over Australia.

After that came a far bigger station called Mir, launched in 1986. Over many years, workers added new sections called modules. It became a real orbiting lab. One crew member stayed aboard for over a year. Mir also survived a fire and a crash with a cargo ship. Its crew kept working anyway. Visitors from far away later came to Mir too, as two nations began working together in space.

These early stations taught engineers countless lessons about living, working, and repairing things far from home.

Years later, engineers combined ideas from Salyut, Skylab, and Mir. They built a new station called the ISS. It still circles Earth today.

versions.title: Space Stations Before the ISS
versions.text:
Long before the ISS existed, no home had ever orbited Earth. Then, in 1971, the Soviets launched Salyut 1, the first space station. It began an era of orbiting labs that led to the ISS.

A crew flew up to Salyut 1 in a small ship. They moved aboard, becoming the first people to live in an orbiting home. Sadly, that mission ended in tragedy when the crew died on the trip home. Even so, the Soviets kept building new Salyut stations. Later missions worked well, with crews staying for weeks or months.

Meanwhile, the United States built its own station called Skylab. Engineers made it from an empty rocket stage. When Skylab launched in 1973, part of its shield tore away. A solar panel jammed, leaving the station without power and dangerously hot. The first crew made emergency repairs, freeing the panel and rigging a shade. Three crews lived and worked aboard Skylab. They studied the Sun and tested how long missions affect the body. By 1979, with no fuel left, Skylab fell and broke apart over Australia.

The Soviets then built a far bigger station called Mir, launched in 1986. Over the next decade, workers added several new modules. Mir became a huge orbiting complex. A cosmonaut set a record there, spending 437 days in space on one mission. Mir also survived a fire and a crash with a cargo ship, yet its crew kept the station running. As old tensions eased, American astronauts began visiting Mir too, a sign of growing cooperation.

All these early stations, with their damage, repairs, and hard-won records, taught engineers key lessons. Those lessons later shaped the design of the ISS.

versions.title: Space Stations Before the ISS
versions.text:
Long before the ISS carried a rotating crew, no home had ever orbited Earth. That changed in 1971. The Soviets launched Salyut 1, the first space station in history. It opened an era of orbiting labs that led to the ISS.

A crew flew up to Salyut 1 aboard a small ship. They moved inside, becoming the first humans ever to live in an orbiting home. Tragically, that mission ended badly. The crew died on the return trip to Earth. Despite this setback, the Soviets pressed on. They launched further Salyut stations. Later versions added a second docking port. This let fresh crews and supply ships arrive while a mission was still underway.

Meanwhile, the United States built its own station, Skylab. Engineers made it from the empty upper stage of a rocket. When Skylab launched in 1973, part of its shield tore away. A solar panel jammed shut. The station lost power and grew dangerously hot inside. The first crew performed urgent repairs during a spacewalk. They freed the panel and rigged a makeshift sunshade. Three crews lived and worked aboard Skylab. They studied the Sun and tested how a long mission affects the body. By 1979, Skylab had no fuel left to raise its orbit. It fell back and scattered debris across Western Australia, harming no one.

The Soviets then built a far larger station, Mir, launched in 1986. Over the next decade, engineers attached several new modules. Mir became a sprawling orbiting complex with several labs. A cosmonaut set a lasting record there, spending 437 days in orbit on one mission. Mir also survived a fire and a serious collision with a cargo ship. Yet its crew managed to keep the station running. As old tensions eased, American astronauts began visiting Mir aboard the Shuttle. This was a sign of growing cooperation between two former rivals.

Together, these early stations, with their damage, repairs, and hard-won records, taught engineers lessons. Those lessons shaped the design of the ISS.

The crew died during their return trip, a loss that shook the Soviet space program. Despite this painful setback, engineers nonetheless pressed on regardless. They launched further Salyut stations throughout the 1970s. Later versions added a second docking port. This let fresh crews and supply ships arrive while a mission was still underway.

A solar panel jammed shut, leaving the station without power and dangerously hot inside. The first crew performed urgent repairs during a spacewalk. They freed the panel and rigged a makeshift sunshade. Three crews lived and worked aboard Skylab, watching the Sun for months. They also tested how a long mission affects the body. By 1979, with no fuel left, Skylab fell back through the sky and scattered debris across Western Australia, harming no one.

versions.title: Space Stations Before the ISS
versions.text:
Long before the ISS began hosting a rotating international crew, no human home had ever orbited Earth. That changed in 1971, when the Soviet Union launched Salyut 1, the first space station in history, opening an era of orbiting laboratories that eventually led to the ISS.

A crew flew up to Salyut 1 aboard a separate spacecraft and transferred inside, becoming the first humans ever to inhabit a home in orbit. Tragically, this pioneering mission ended in disaster when the crew died during their return to Earth, a loss that profoundly affected the Soviet space program. Despite this setback, engineers pressed forward, launching additional Salyut stations throughout the 1970s. Later versions added a second docking port. This let fresh crews and supply vehicles arrive while a mission remained underway, extending each station's operational duration.

Meanwhile, the United States built its own station, Skylab, by converting the empty upper stage of a rocket into a functioning laboratory. When Skylab launched in 1973, part of its shield tore away and a solar panel jammed shut. The station lost power and grew dangerously overheated inside. The first crew carried out urgent repairs during a dramatic spacewalk, freeing the panel and rigging a makeshift sunshade. Three crews lived and worked aboard Skylab, observing the Sun for months and studying how a mission of extended duration affects the human body. By 1979, having run out of fuel, Skylab fell back through the atmosphere and scattered debris across Western Australia, harming no one.

The Soviet Union then built a far larger station, Mir, launched in 1986. Over the following decade, engineers attached several modules, including Kvant and Spektr, transforming Mir into a sprawling orbiting complex. A cosmonaut set an enduring record there, spending 437 consecutive days in orbit during one mission, still the longest spaceflight completed by one person. Mir also survived an onboard fire and a serious collision with an uncrewed cargo vehicle that punctured one module, yet its crew managed to keep the station operating. As old tensions eased in the 1990s, American astronauts began visiting Mir aboard the Space Shuttle, a symbol of growing cooperation between two former rivals.

Together, these early stations left behind a profound legacy. Their damage, repairs, and hard-won records taught engineers lessons that shaped both the design and the cooperative spirit of the ISS.

versions.title: Space Stations Before the ISS
versions.text:
Long before the ISS began hosting a continuously rotating international crew, no human home had ever orbited Earth at all. That changed dramatically in 1971, when the Soviet Union launched Salyut 1, the first space station in history, opening an entire era of orbiting laboratories that eventually culminated in the ISS.

A crew flew up to Salyut 1 aboard a separate spacecraft and transferred inside, becoming the first humans ever to inhabit a home in orbit, however briefly. Tragically, this pioneering mission ended in disaster when the crew died during their return to Earth, a devastating loss that profoundly affected the Soviet space program. Despite this setback, engineers pressed forward regardless, launching additional Salyut stations throughout the 1970s. Later versions incorporated a second docking port. This seemingly small change enabled fresh crews and supply vehicles to arrive mid-mission. It dramatically extended each station's operational duration.

Meanwhile, the United States constructed its own station, Skylab, by converting the empty upper stage of a Saturn V rocket into a functioning laboratory, an inventive and economical solution. When Skylab launched in 1973, part of its shield tore away and a solar panel jammed shut. The station grew critically short of power and dangerously overheated inside. The first crew carried out urgent repairs during a dramatic spacewalk, freeing the stuck panel and rigging a makeshift sunshade. Three crews lived and worked aboard Skylab, observing the Sun for months and studying how a mission of extended duration affects the human body. By 1979, having exhausted its fuel, Skylab fell back through the atmosphere and scattered debris across Western Australia, harming no one.

The Soviet Union subsequently built a far larger station, Mir, launched in 1986, intended to grow over time rather than remain fixed. Over the following decade, engineers attached several additional modules, including Kvant and Spektr, gradually transforming Mir into a sprawling orbiting complex with multiple laboratories. A cosmonaut set an enduring record there, spending 437 consecutive days in orbit during a single mission, still the longest continuous spaceflight ever completed by one person. Mir also survived an onboard fire and a serious collision with a cargo vehicle that punctured one module. Yet its crew somehow managed to keep the station operating. As old tensions gradually eased during the 1990s, American astronauts began visiting Mir aboard the Space Shuttle, a powerful symbol of growing cooperation between two former rivals.

Together, these early stations left behind a profound and lasting legacy. Their accumulated damage, improvised repairs, and hard-won records taught engineers lessons that ultimately shaped both the design and the cooperative spirit of the station that followed them.

versions.title: Space Stations Before the ISS
versions.text:
Long before the ISS began hosting a continuously rotating international crew, no human home had ever orbited Earth at all, a fact that seems almost unbelievable from today's vantage point. That changed dramatically in 1971, when the Soviet Union launched Salyut 1, the first space station in history and a genuinely pioneering achievement, one that opened an entire era of orbiting laboratories eventually culminating, decades later, in the ISS itself.

A crew flew up to Salyut 1 aboard a separate spacecraft and transferred inside, becoming, however briefly, the first humans ever to inhabit a home in orbit. Tragically, this pioneering mission ended in disaster when the crew died during their return to Earth, a devastating loss that profoundly affected the Soviet space program for years afterward and forced engineers to redesign their spacecraft's safety systems. Despite this setback, engineers pressed forward regardless, launching additional Salyut stations throughout the remainder of the 1970s. Later versions incorporated a second docking port, a seemingly small change. It nevertheless enabled fresh crews and uncrewed supply vehicles to arrive mid-mission, dramatically extending each station's operational duration and scientific output.

Meanwhile, on the other side of the world, the United States constructed its own station, Skylab, by converting the empty upper stage of a powerful Saturn V rocket into a functioning laboratory, an inventive and economical solution born partly from leftover Apollo-era hardware. When Skylab launched in 1973, part of its protective shield tore away and a solar panel jammed shut. The station was left critically short of power and dangerously overheated almost immediately after reaching orbit. The first crew carried out urgent repairs during a dramatic spacewalk, freeing the stuck panel and rigging a makeshift sunshade before irreversible damage occurred. Three separate crews eventually lived and worked aboard Skylab, observing the Sun for months at a stretch and studying how a mission of extended duration affects the human body in ways no one had previously measured. By 1979, having exhausted the fuel needed to raise its decaying orbit, Skylab finally fell back through the atmosphere and scattered debris across Western Australia, harming no one, though it briefly made headlines worldwide.

The Soviet Union subsequently built a far larger station, Mir, launched in 1986 and intended from the outset to grow steadily over time rather than remain fixed. Over the following decade, engineers attached several additional modules, including Kvant and Spektr, one at a time, gradually transforming Mir into a sprawling orbiting complex with multiple specialized laboratories. A cosmonaut set an enduring record there, spending 437 consecutive days in orbit during a single mission, still the longest continuous spaceflight ever completed by one person. Mir also survived both an onboard fire and a serious collision with a cargo vehicle that punctured one module, patched by the crew with whatever materials they had on hand. As old tensions gradually eased throughout the 1990s, American astronauts began visiting Mir aboard the Space Shuttle, a powerful symbol of growing cooperation between two nations that had so recently been bitter rivals.

Together, these early stations left behind a profound and lasting legacy: their accumulated damage, improvised repairs, and hard-won records taught engineers countless practical lessons that ultimately shaped both the physical design and the cooperative, international spirit of the space station that followed them, one that still orbits Earth today.

versions.title: Space Stations Before the ISS
versions.text:
Long before the International Space Station began hosting a continuously rotating international crew representing more than a dozen nations, no human home had ever orbited Earth at all, a fact that seems almost unbelievable from today's vantage point, given how routine spaceflight has since become. That changed dramatically in 1971, when the Soviet Union launched Salyut 1, the first space station in history and a genuinely pioneering achievement, one that opened an entire era of orbiting laboratories eventually culminating, decades later, in the ISS itself.

A crew flew up to Salyut 1 aboard a separate spacecraft and transferred inside, becoming, however briefly, the first humans ever to inhabit a home in orbit rather than merely visit space for a few hours. Tragically, this pioneering mission ended in disaster when the crew died during their return to Earth, a devastating loss that profoundly affected the Soviet space program for years afterward and forced engineers to redesign their spacecraft's safety systems from the ground up. Despite this setback, engineers pressed forward regardless, launching additional Salyut stations throughout the remainder of the 1970s. Later versions, particularly Salyut 6 and Salyut 7, incorporated a second docking port, a seemingly small change that nevertheless enabled fresh crews and uncrewed supply vehicles to arrive while a mission remained underway, which in turn dramatically extended each station's operational duration and overall scientific output.

Meanwhile, on the other side of the world, the United States constructed its own station, Skylab, by converting the empty upper stage of a powerful Saturn V rocket into a functioning laboratory, an inventive and remarkably economical solution born partly from leftover hardware from the Apollo Moon program. When Skylab launched in 1973, part of its protective shield tore away and a solar panel jammed shut, leaving the station critically short of power and dangerously overheated inside almost immediately after reaching orbit. The first crew carried out urgent repairs during a dramatic spacewalk, freeing the stuck panel and rigging a makeshift sunshade to cool the overheated interior before irreversible damage could occur. Three separate crews eventually lived and worked aboard Skylab, observing the Sun for months at a stretch and studying how a mission of extended duration affects the human body in ways no one had previously measured with such precision. By 1979, having exhausted the fuel needed to raise its steadily decaying orbit, Skylab finally fell back through the atmosphere and scattered debris across Western Australia, fortunately harming no one in the process, though the event briefly made headlines around the world.

The Soviet Union subsequently built a far larger station, Mir, launched in 1986 and intended from the outset to grow steadily over time rather than remain fixed in its original configuration. Over the following decade, engineers attached several additional modules, including Kvant and Spektr, one at a time, gradually transforming Mir into a sprawling orbiting complex containing multiple specialized laboratories. Cosmonaut Valeri Polyakov set an enduring record there, spending 437 consecutive days in orbit during a single mission, still the longest continuous spaceflight ever completed by one person. Mir also survived both an onboard fire and a serious collision with an uncrewed cargo vehicle that punctured one module, yet its determined crews somehow managed to keep the station operating and complete their planned research regardless, patching the leak with whatever materials they had close at hand. As Cold War tensions gradually eased throughout the 1990s, American astronauts began visiting Mir aboard the Space Shuttle, a powerful symbol of growing cooperation between two nations that had so recently been bitter rivals on Earth.

Together, these early stations left behind a profound and lasting legacy: their accumulated damage, improvised repairs, and hard-won records taught engineers countless practical lessons that ultimately shaped both the physical design and the cooperative, international spirit of the space station that followed them, one that still circles Earth today, carrying forward the achievements of its pioneering predecessors.

MID.modelAnswer: One important lesson came from Skylab, whose protective shield tore away during launch and left the station dangerously overheated. HIGH.prompt: The article describes both setbacks (like the Salyut 1 tragedy and the Skylab and Mir incidents) and achievements of early space stations. Explain how these early stations' legacy shaped the ISS, using at least two pieces of evidence.
checklist: I explained what legacy these stations left.
I gave at least two pieces of evidence.
I connected the evidence to the ISS.
HIGH.modelAnswer: The legacy of Salyut, Skylab, and Mir was the hard-won knowledge of how to live, repair, and cooperate in space, which later shaped the ISS. Skylab's torn shield and jammed solar panel forced engineers to learn how to perform urgent repairs during spacewalks, a skill that remains essential on the ISS today. Mir's long stays, including Valeri Polyakov's 437-day mission, and its survival of a fire and a collision, showed that determined crews could keep a damaged station running, while the later Shuttle-Mir cooperation between the United States and Russia became a direct model for the international partnership that now runs the ISS.
